entities.summary:
Bérenger Frédol, a French canon lawyer, rose to prominence in the late 13th century as a Cardinal-Bishop of Frascati, playing a key role in the Catholic Church's governance. His appointment by Pope Gregory X in 1276 was significant, as it marked a turning point in the Church's relations with European monarchs. Frédol's tenure was marked by controversy, including a dispute with the Holy Roman Emperor, Frederick II, over ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Despite this, he remained a powerful figure in the Church, influencing the development of canon law and the appointment of future Cardinals. Frédol's legacy is also marked by his involvement in the translation of the Bible into vernacular languages, a move that would have far-reaching consequences for European literature and culture. Through his work, Frédol helped pave the way for the Protestant Reformation, which would reshape the course of Western history. His influence can also be seen in the rise of humanism, which emphasized the study of classical texts and the pursuit of individual knowledge. In the end, Frédol's life and work serve as a testament to the enduring power of the Catholic Church in medieval Europe, and the complex web of relationships that bound Church and state together.

Frédol was born in the late 13th century, the exact date unknown, and died on June 19, 1323. His life and career spanned a time of great upheaval in Europe, marked by the ongoing struggle between Church and state, the rise of nation-states, and the emergence of a new class of intellectuals who would shape the course of Western civilization. Through his work, Frédol helped shape the intellectual and cultural landscape of medieval Europe, leaving behind a legacy that would continue to influence the Church and society for centuries to come.

entities.summary:
Berengar Fredol or Bérenger Frédol was a French canon lawyer and Cardinal-Bishop of Frascati.
He played a significant role in shaping the Catholic Church's legal and administrative structures during the late Middle Ages.
Born in 1250 in France, Fredol rose to prominence through his education at the University of Paris and his appointment as a canon at the Notre-Dame Cathedral.

As a key figure in the Curia Romana, Fredol contributed to the development of the Canon Law, a collection of ecclesiastical laws that governed the Church's internal affairs.
He also participated in several synods and councils, including the Council of Vienne, where he played a crucial role in resolving theological disputes.

Fredol's legacy extends beyond his contributions to the Canon Law, as he also helped establish the office of the Cardinal-Bishop of Frascati, a position that would become increasingly powerful during the Renaissance.
This institution became a hub for papal politics and a center of influence for the Catholic Church in Italy.

The legacy of Berengar Fredol can be seen in the continued relevance of the Canon Law, which remains an important part of Catholic canon.
The modern Catholic Church still uses many of the principles established by Fredol during his time as Cardinal-Bishop of Frascati.
